If no $$$0$$$ exists, then Bessie obviously wins, and if no $$$1$$$ exists, then Elsie obviously wins. If a $$$0$$$ and $$$1$$$ both exist on Bessie's turn, then she can remove a $$$0$$$, and similarly if a $$$0$$$ and $$$1$$$ both exist on Elsie's turn, then she can remove a $$$1$$$. Thus if the number of $$$1$$$s >= number of $$$0$$$s, Bessie will win, since she can always ensure that the number of $$$1$$$s is >= the number of $$$0$$$s. If the number of $$$1$$$s is < the number of $$$0$$$s, then no matter what Bessie does on her turn, the game will be flipped to Elsie having this same winning position, so she will lose.

Each number can be the minimum element of at most a row and a column, so we must have $$$n \leq k$$$. Additionally, note that $$$1$$$ is always the minimum element of its row and column, so we must have $$$k \leq 2n-1$$$. We claim that it is always possible to construct a satisfying matrix for $$$n \leq k \leq 2n-1$$$. Let $$$x = k+1-n$$$ — then $$$1 \leq x \leq n$$$. Then, place $$$1, \ldots, x$$$ in the first row, place $$$x+1, \ldots, 2x - 1$$$ in the first column below the $$$1$$$, and place $$$2x, \ldots, k$$$ on the main diagonal outside of the top-left $$$x \times x$$$ box as follows: $$$$$$\begin{bmatrix} 1 & \cdots & x & & & \\ x+1 & & & & & \\ \vdots & & & & & \\ 2x-1 & & & & & \\ & & & 2x & & \\ & & & & \ddots & \\ & & & & & k \\ \end{bmatrix}$$$$$$ Each row or column contains at least one of these numbers and achieves $$$|f(A)| = k$$$ , so we can fill in the blank spaces with numbers $$$k+1, \ldots, n^2$$$ however we wish.

Say $$$f(A, k) = x$$$. Then we know that $$$S$$$ contains at least one number in each of the intervals $$$[0, k-1], [k, 2k-1], ..., [k(x-1), kx-1]$$$, but no number in the interval $$$[kx, k(x+1)-1]$$$ — call this last one a bad range. Now, let us try greedily including every number we can in $$$[0, n]$$$. The only reason why we cannot include a number is if it is in a bad range. We can keep track of all these bad ranges using a prefix sum, (e.g., for $$$f(A, k) = x$$$, increment $$$p[kx]$$$, decrement $$$p[k(x+1)]$$$, and prefix sum over $$$p$$$). Then we include a number if and only if $$$p[i] = 0$$$. This is the best possible scenario, as we include every number possible, and it will result in a valid $$$B$$$ since Farmer John only gives you arrays where $$$B$$$ exists.

To extend the previous solution, remember that we are given various good intervals (where we must include at least one number) and bad intervals (where we must include no numbers), and any valid $$$B$$$ must satisfy all of them. We first discard all good intervals that completely contain another good interval, since satisfying the inner interval automatically satisfies the outer one. We will be left with at most $$$n$$$ intervals, since all the right endpoints will be distinct. If you sort these intervals, we can make the observation that including a number will satisfy a range of these intervals. We can use a simple DP maintaining the last satisfied interval while looping through numbers $$$0$$$ to $$$n-1$$$, being careful not to consider any numbers in bad intervals (we can check this using prefix sums as in the solution to C1). There are $$$O(n \log{n})$$$ intervals, and we can speed up the DP using prefix sums to compute this in $$$O(n \log {n})$$$; the total complexity will be $$$O(n \log^2 {n})$$$ due to sorting.

Reverse the removals so they become insertions. Maintain the set $$$S$$$ of indices of the opponents that the champion forfeits to. When inserting a champion at $$$i$$$, consider the largest element $$$j \lt i$$$, where $$$j \in S$$$. If we take the sum of all the active warriors' skills from $$$j$$$ to $$$i-1$$$, that will be the skill level of the champion fighting $$$i$$$. If this sum is less than $$$a_i$$$, then we insert $$$i$$$ into the set, and update $$$j = i$$$. Now, note that the current champions skill (after fighting $$$a_i$$$) has increased from before, and so we look at elements greater than $$$i$$$ in the set, and test if the champion skill loses to $$$a_i$$$ by seeing if the sum of skills from $$$j$$$ to $$$i-1$$$ is less than $$$a_i$$$. This requires a BIT/segment tree to query sums and process additions quickly.

Let $$$M=a_n$$$. For a rearrangement $$$b$$$, construct a directed graph whose vertices are the island values. If the suffix maximum at the position of value $$$v$$$ is $$$s$$$, its only possible outgoing edge is $$$v\to s-v$$$. This edge exists only if $$$s-v$$$ is one of the island values.
This means every node has at most one outgoing edge, and $$$b$$$ is good if there is some directed path which visits all nodes.
First, we will show that a good rearrangement has exactly $$$2$$$ suffix maxima.

Suppose a good rearrangement had one suffix max. That must be $$$M$$$, and therefore, every node goes from $$$x \to M - x$$$. Continuing the path, it goes $$$x \to M - x \to x$$$, creating a cycle. Therefore, you can only visit at most 2 nodes. Since $$$n \geq 4$$$, this rearrangement cannot be good.

Suppose a good rearrangement had more than $$$2$$$ suffix maxima. Each suffix max will point to $$$0$$$, and so there are at least $$$3$$$ edges pointing to $$$0$$$. Because a directed path must exist if it was good, that directed path takes $$$n - 1$$$ edges. Since this directed path does not revisit nodes, this path can contain at most one of the edges which goes to $$$0$$$. Since there are at least $$$2$$$ edges not on the directed path, there are at least $$$n-1 + 2 = n + 1$$$ edges in the graph, which is greater than the number of nodes. Since every node has at most one outgoing edge, this is impossible.
Therefore, there are exactly $$$2$$$ suffix maxima. Since the largest number and the last number must both be suffix maxima, we know the two are $$$M$$$ and $$$b_n$$$.

We next show that $$$0$$$ must appear before $$$M$$$. Otherwise, no vertex points to $$$M$$$, so the path must start at $$$M$$$. It then follows $$$M\to0\to b_n\to0$$$, visiting at most three distinct vertices, which is impossible since $$$n\ge4$$$.

Therefore, $$$0\to M$$$. If $$$M$$$ were not the final vertex of the path, then either its predecessor would be $$$0$$$, forcing a repeated visit in $$$0\to M\to0$$$, or the path would start with $$$M\to0\to M$$$. Both are impossible. Thus, the path must end with $$$0\to M$$$.

We can now build the path backwards. The predecessor of $$$0$$$ must be $$$b_n$$$, giving $$$b_n\to0\to M$$$. The predecessor of $$$b_n$$$ must then be $$$M-b_n$$$, since the other possibility, $$$0$$$, is already used. Continuing this way, the transformations alternate.
Let $$$x=M-b_n$$$ and $$$k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor$$$. The backwards sequence is

The values $$$0,x,\dots,(k-1)x$$$ must appear before $$$M$$$, and the remaining values other than $$$M$$$ must appear after $$$M$$$, with $$$b_n=M-x$$$ last. Both groups can otherwise be shuffled arbitrarily. Conversely, any such ordering has suffix maximum $$$M$$$ before $$$M$$$ and $$$b_n$$$ after it, so the backwards sequence above gives a valid path. Therefore, whenever the first $$$n$$$ values of this sequence match the input values after sorting, the number of corresponding rearrangements is $$$k!(n-k-2)!$$$.

We only need to test $$$x=M-a_{n-1}$$$ and $$$x=M-a_{n-2}$$$. Otherwise, $$$b_n=M-x \lt a_{n-2}$$$. Both $$$a_{n-1}$$$ and $$$a_{n-2}$$$ must then belong to the group of multiples of $$$x$$$, but $$$0 \lt a_{n-1}-a_{n-2} \lt M-a_{n-2} \lt x,$$$ which is impossible for two distinct multiples of $$$x$$$.

Obviously, if any $$$a[i] \gt b[i]$$$, we have an impossible case.
Consider the SCCs $$$S_k$$$ of the graph where $$$i$$$ has an out-edge to $$$j$$$ for all $$$a[i] \leq j \leq b[i]$$$.

Firstly, we can "compress" all nodes where $$$a[i] = b[i]$$$. That is, if $$$i$$$ has an edge to $$$j$$$ where $$$a[j] = b[j]$$$, point $$$i$$$ to $$$b[j]$$$ instead. Any SCCs consisting only of these nodes can be ignored, but all other SCCs must be visited.

Now consider the modified condensation graph, where we draw an edge from $$$S_k$$$ to $$$S_l$$$ for $$$k \neq l$$$ whenever there is $$$i \in S_k$$$ and $$$b[i] \in S_l$$$. Then we can impose some more conditions:

1. There cannot exist two out-edges from any SCC. This is because we must visit one of the nodes in $$$S_k$$$, say $$$i$$$, increment and go to $$$b[i]$$$, and then we cannot return to $$$j$$$ to increment it to $$$b[j]$$$.
2. Using similar logic, the modified condensation graph formed by the remaining SCCs must be a chain — this is the only way we can visit and fix all the nodes in every SCC.

3. Using similar logic again, there must be at most one node with $$$a[i] \lt i = b[i]$$$. If there is $$$i \neq j$$$ that fits this description, then we must for example fix $$$i$$$ first, and then we are stuck at $$$i$$$ forever.

4. Consider the one node in an SCC which contains an out-edge. This is the last node visited and fixed in the SCC (since we cannot return after that). However, since $$$i \leq b[i]$$$, we cannot fix all succeeding nodes in the SCC and then return to this node, so the node containing the out-edge must be the greatest labeled node in the SCC.
We now show a valid construction for all arrays satisfying these restrictions.

Let $$$c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_{|S_k|}$$$ be the nodes in SCC $$$S_k$$$. First, construct a directed tree containing all $$$c_i$$$ that points towards $$$c_1$$$ — this can be constructed by reversing all internal edges and running a DFS. Whatever node $$$i$$$ we are on, we can lazily increment $$$a[i]$$$ to match the edge of our tree and make our way to $$$c_1$$$, then fix $$$a[c_1]$$$ to $$$b[c_1]$$$ and move to $$$b[c_1]$$$. Now to update the directed tree root at $$$c_2$$$, we only need to point the children of $$$c_1$$$ to $$$c_2$$$. This must be possible due to the condition $$$i \leq b[i]$$$, and we can repeat this for all nodes in the SCC. We need to use operation $$$2$$$ at most $$$n$$$ times for each node to traverse to it, and we need to use operation $$$1$$$ at most $$$n$$$ times for each node to increment $$$a[i]$$$ to $$$b[i]$$$, so this construction is at most $$$2n^2$$$ operations.
With this, you can prove a significantly simpler solution. We will add this proof later.

The individual substrings $$$a$$$, $$$c$$$, and $$$e$$$ do not have to be balanced.

This motivates giving each chosen pairing a region: for the outermost pair, this represents the concatenation $$$ace$$$, and for the inner pairs, these are $$$b$$$ and $$$d$$$, respectively. We also count everything outside all chosen pairings as one region, giving $$$k+1$$$ regions in total.

When rotating, we move each region together with its fillings and insertion counts. Since every ordered choice of region sizes is included in our count, these rotations stay within the configurations we are counting. Therefore, exactly a $$$\frac{1}{k+1}$$$ fraction give valid structures.

To compute the required coefficients for all $$$k$$$, repeatedly multiply by $$$P(x)$$$, discarding terms of degree greater than $$$n$$$. With FFT, this takes $$$O(n^2\log n)$$$ time; with ordinary polynomial multiplication, it takes $$$O(n^3)$$$ time. The final inclusion-exclusion step takes $$$O(n^2)$$$ time. The $$$O(n^3)$$$ solution is only required here, but there are faster solutions (including a $$$O(n \log^2 n)$$$ sol).
The proof of the cyclic lemma is standard, so we omit it here.
All linear algebra below is over $$$\mathbb{F}_2$$$. We will use two facts:

Construct a bipartite graph with $$$n$$$ row vertices and $$$n$$$ column vertices, where $$$M_{i,j}=1$$$ corresponds to an edge between row $$$i$$$ and column $$$j$$$. By the determinant expansion, $$$\det(M)$$$ is the number of perfect matchings in this graph modulo $$$2$$$.

Let $$$X$$$ be the number of ones initially in $$$M$$$. Since we can erase at most $$$n$$$ ones per move, we need at least $$$\lceil X/n\rceil$$$ moves. We will achieve this bound by maintaining $$$\operatorname{rank}(M)=n$$$ until the final two moves.
First, consider the case $$$X\leq 3n$$$, where $$$X$$$ now denotes the current number of ones.

Since $$$\det(M)=1$$$, the bipartite graph has a perfect matching. Equivalently, there is a permutation $$$p$$$ such that $$$M_{i,p_i}=1$$$ for every $$$i$$$. Permute the columns so that these ones lie on the main diagonal.
There are $$$X-n$$$ ones outside the diagonal. Choose whichever side of the diagonal contains fewer ones, and erase all of them. This erases at most
ones and makes the matrix upper or lower triangular. Since every diagonal entry is $$$1$$$, the matrix still has rank $$$n$$$.

If there are enough off-diagonal ones, continue erasing them until we have erased exactly $$$n$$$ ones. The matrix remains triangular with diagonal entries equal to $$$1$$$, so it remains full rank. We can then undo the column permutation.

Otherwise, erase all off-diagonal ones and enough diagonal ones to complete the move. The remaining ones lie on distinct diagonal positions, so their number equals the remaining rank. We can erase all of them on the next move. If only the $$$n$$$ diagonal ones remain initially, we simply erase them in one move.
Thus, this case achieves the lower bound, with rank decreasing only during the final two moves.
Now consider the case $$$X \gt 3n$$$. We will erase exactly $$$n$$$ ones while preserving full rank.
First, we show how to erase two ones while preserving the determinant whenever the current matrix has more than $$$2n$$$ ones.
By pigeonhole, some column contains at least three ones. For each corresponding edge $$$e$$$, let $$$q(e)$$$ be the number of perfect matchings containing $$$e$$$, modulo $$$2$$$.
Among three edges, two have the same value of $$$q(e)$$$. Since they belong to the same column, no perfect matching contains both. Erasing these two edges therefore changes the determinant by
modulo $$$2$$$. Hence, the matrix remains full rank.
For even $$$n$$$, repeatedly apply this operation until we have erased $$$n$$$ ones. Since we started with more than $$$3n$$$ ones, the matrix has more than $$$2n$$$ ones throughout the move.
For odd $$$n$$$, we first need to erase an odd number of ones while preserving the determinant. Afterwards, we can finish the move by repeatedly erasing pairs.

Choose two columns $$$c$$$ and $$$d$$$ sharing a one in some row $$$r$$$. Such a pair exists because some row contains at least two ones. Try erasing each one in these two columns individually. If any such removal preserves the determinant, erase that one and continue with pair removals.
Otherwise, every edge in these columns belongs to an odd number of perfect matchings. We will show that some L-shaped triple can be erased instead.
and consider an edge $$$g=(i,c)$$$ with $$$i\neq r$$$. These three edges form an L, whose ends are $$$f$$$ and $$$g$$$.
No perfect matching contains both $$$e$$$ and $$$f$$$, or both $$$e$$$ and $$$g$$$. Therefore, by inclusion-exclusion, the number of perfect matchings destroyed by erasing the L is
where $$$q(f,g)$$$ counts perfect matchings containing both ends, modulo $$$2$$$.
The first three terms are all $$$1$$$, so the determinant is preserved exactly when $$$q(f,g)=1$$$.
Every perfect matching containing $$$f$$$ uses exactly one edge from column $$$c$$$. That edge cannot be $$$e$$$, since $$$e$$$ and $$$f$$$ share a row. Consequently,
Since $$$q(f)=1$$$, at least one term is $$$1$$$. Thus, at least one of these L-shaped triples preserves the determinant when erased.
For odd $$$n$$$, we therefore erase either one one or three ones, then repeatedly erase pairs until we have erased exactly $$$n$$$ ones. Again, the matrix stays full rank throughout.
Combining the two cases gives an algorithm using exactly $$$\lceil X/n\rceil$$$ moves.
To implement it, we can test a proposed removal by temporarily erasing the chosen entries and running Gaussian elimination in $$$O(n^3)$$$ time.

For each pair removal, choose three ones in a column and test their three possible pairs. In an odd-sized move, we test only the ones in the two selected columns, followed by the L-shaped triples using the fixed edges $$$e$$$ and $$$f$$$. This requires $$$O(n)$$$ tests per odd-sized move.

There are $$$O(n)$$$ moves and $$$O(n^2)$$$ pair removals overall, so the total number of determinant tests is $$$O(n^2)$$$. The perfect matching needed in the final phase can be found in $$$O(n^3)$$$ time.
Therefore, the total complexity is $$$O(n^5)$$$. Using bitsets for Gaussian elimination gives the usual $$$O(n^5/w)$$$ bitset bound, where $$$w$$$ is the machine word size.

To optimize from $$$O(n^5/w)$$$ to $$$O(n^4/w)$$$, we need to use some Linear Algebra. Instead of recomputing the determinant in $$$O(n^3/w)$$$ to test removals and after removals, we can use something called

We will first prove that for any row/column of a rank $$$n$$$ matrix, we can zero out everything in that row/column except one, and maintain rank $$$n$$$. This is because rank $$$n$$$ means the determinant is $$$1$$$, so there are exactly an odd number of perfect matchings in total (read Solution 1 for more understanding). Therefore at least $$$1$$$ of the ones in the row/column must be in an odd number of perfect matchings (since if they were all even then the total number would be even). This means if we delete all other ones but that one, then we would keep rank $$$n$$$.

This actually all you need to prove to solve the problem. Note that after we clear out one row except one number, we can clear out that column except that one number (even partially) and the determinant will not change (and the same works when clearing out a column with the leftover row).

For every turn, we want to try to find $$$n$$$ things to remove without changing the rank. Therefore, we begin by finding the one in the biggest row/column we can keep while removing everything else. Then we remove everything in the column/row of that one, and the everything in the row/column into the queue. If the queue + the current removals is big enough to reach $$$n$$$ removals, then we can just remove the ones in the queue. If the queue is too small, then we repeat one the next biggest row/column. Because the queue contains the row/column with the most ones, when the current removals will never exceed $$$n$$$ if the the queue + current removals is less than $$$n$$$. Once we run out of row/columns to clear, we can start removing the ones we excluded removing, since we have to reduce the rank at this point.

To find the one we must keep, you have to utilize the inverse, since we can clear out the row/column on $$$M_{i, j}$$$ if $$$M^{-1}_{j, i} = 1$$$ (proof is by Cramer's Rule). We can keep track of the inverse after this clear out operation in $$$O(n^2 / w)$$$ if done properly (using something similar to Woodbury Matrix Identity, look at Solution 1 for details). If implemented properly, this results in a $$$O(n^3 / w)$$$ solution.
